bet.dominantBottleneck: The team treats published lift coefficients as authoritative for their specific wing shapes, yet their own gliders underperform these tables by a large margin and wing enlargement/curvature did not fix it. The core blocking issue is that lift prediction is wrong—not control or power—so the next action must directly measure how lift actually scales with their own wings.

routes.route: Build a whirling-arm or fan-driven measurement rig to measure actual lift of their own wing sections on a mechanical balance and compare against the published coefficients
routes.reason: Discriminates directly between 'published tables wrong for these shapes' vs 'build/rig error', since their full gliders underpredict lift. Capability allows simple balances and a fan/wind apparatus. Cheap and low-risk compared to powered prototypes.

routes.route: Conduct systematic small-model wing tests at varying sizes, curvatures and aspect ratios to map where the published coefficients diverge and calibrate their own correction factor
routes.reason: Bounded within available small-model testing and directly tests the generalization boundary between small models and full-size, which the rival's success also hinges on. Produces a usable scale-correction rather than a one-off check.

routes.route: Pursue powered full-size prototype scaling to close the gap with the rival institution
routes.reason: Expensive and dangerous, and without resolving the lift-underprediction the powered prototype would fly no better than the gliders; it amplifies rather than diagnoses the bottleneck.

routes.route: Modify control surfaces / wing-warping further to improve control
routes.reason: Evidence says control already works in tests and enlarging wings introduced control problems; control is not the dominant bottleneck and should only be revisited for the new wing configuration after lift measurement.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Distinguishing whether the null result reflects the absence of an ether reference frame, a cancellation with a compensating physical effect (material deformation or entrainment), or a breakdown of the assumed moving-frame kinematic transformation — the current null observation alone cannot separate these, and modern atomic clocks/lasers are unavailable to give independent kinematic handles.

routes.route: Null-ether / Lorentz-relativistic kinematics: reinterpret the moving-frame transformation so that the interferometer rest frame is physically equivalent to the ether, keeping Maxwellian electrodynamics intact.
routes.reason: This route preserves the empirically powerful electrodynamic phenomena while reworking lengths/time consistently; the null is its natural prediction. However its full validation needs independent tests beyond the single rotating-null experiment, since one null cannot certify all features.

routes.route: Compensating material deformation: invoke physical contraction/strain of the interferometer (FitzGerald-type) that exactly cancels the predicted optical path difference.
routes.reason: Directly testable in principle since it predicts measurable mechanical/optical changes in other configurations (e.g., different materials or construction); currently unconstrained so deserves an independent discriminating probe rather than assumption.

routes.route: Partial/complete ether entrainment by matter near Earth and its optical paths.
routes.reason: Logically possible and would explain the null at Earth's surface, but is constrained by existing astronomical aberration observations and is hard to reconcile globally; needs a test that distinguishes local entrainment from universal ether rest.

routes.route: Scaling/sensitivity interplay: accept a tiny residual far below current resolution and push sensitivity/apparatus reconfiguration to see whether any directional shift appears at larger effective optical path.
routes.reason: Valuable as a confirming probe but low priority because the current apparatus already exceeds prior null sensitivity and the question is now theoretical discrimination, not mere magnitude resolution.

routes.route: Seeking a decisive discriminator between contraction and kinematic relativity using a differently oriented/configured interferometer (e.g., asymmetrical arms) or a different physical observable sensitive to length changes but not frame kinematics.
routes.reason: This is the most discriminating next step: a contraction hypothesis ties compensation to material properties and arm geometry, whereas relativistic kinematics predicts universality; testing with varied materials/arm configurations can separate them.

Run each at multiple orientations and seasons (Earth velocity varies), and cross-check each against known astronomical aberration magnitudes to rule out partial-entrainment compensation.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Distinguishing among three families of explanation for the second-order ether-drift null: (a) ether partially/fully entrained so Earth drags the medium locally, (b) material/geometric compensation through length contraction or deformation that restores the null while preserving moving-frame kinematics, and (c) breakdown of the reference-medium interpretation requiring a new kinematic framework (no accessible direct probe of the medium makes these hard to separate observationally).

routes.reason: If a small residual ether-motion signal depends on Earth's orbital velocity component, its seasonal modulation distinguishes a genuine ether-drift residual from apparatus-constant systematic artifacts. routes.route: Fringe-width/length-contraction hypothesis test via asymmetric optical path
routes.reason: A hypothesis family says the null arises from physical length contraction/deformation along the direction of motion. routes.route: Extend the moving-line principle to the full chassis in a single paced flow
routes.reason: Whole chassis is much larger than the pilot subassembly and has highly uneven task times; a single paced line couples every station so one mismatch halts downstream flow, which the evidence says is the key risk.

routes.route: Keep stationary flexible teams but add moving-flow only for high-volume subassemblies
routes.reason: Retains flexible fitting/rework capability that the stationary system is proven to supply, while capturing the throughput gain the pilot demonstrated on the subassembly; lowers line-coupling risk for the whole chassis.

routes.route: Adopt moving flow with deliberately unbalanced buffer/feeder stations between uneven tasks
routes.reason: Directly attacks the dominant bottleneck: buffers decouple uneven task times so a mismatch at one station need not halt downstream flow, and powered conveyors/carts are already available.

routes.route: Pursue only tighter part interchangeability before any line change
routes.reason: Interchangeability is necessary but the evidence marks it imperfect; deferring all motion work until it is perfect forfeits the demonstrated throughput gain and the pilot already worked under the current tolerance regime.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Line stoppage coupling: imperfect part interchangeability plus uneven task times means a mismatch at one station can halt the whole downstream moving-flow line, undermining the throughput gain shown in the subassembly pilot.

routes.route: Station-balancing with buffers/wip-in-transit and pacing via powered/gravity conveyance
routes.reason: The subassembly trial already demonstrated the throughput win; the discriminating question is whether it survives chassis-scale uneven task times. Buffers between stations and paced conveyance let fast stations absorb slow ones, decoupling stoppages. This directly tests the dominant bottleneck with the available powered-conveyor capability.

routes.route: Tolerance/gauging upgrade for full interchangeability before line expansion
routes.reason: Interchangeability is a necessary enabler, but the subassembly trial succeeded with imperfect interchangeability, and the system already relies on flexible rework teams. Pursuing perfect gauging before proving the line is affordable is premature; the flexible-fee team route (below) can carry the residual mismatch risk.

routes.route: Retain flexible local fitting/rework teams on a moving line (hybrid)
routes.reason: This addresses worker rework variable work complements the line. Evidence says the stationary system is flexible for fitting/rework; keeping a small repair crew while moving the main flow preserves that advantage and absorbs the 'mismatch halts flow' risk without needing perfect tolerances. Cheaper and lower-risk than full re-gauging.

routes.route: Job-enrichment / rotation to counter narrow-repetitive turnover
routes.reason: Turnover is a real secondary objective, but it is a cost/experience effect that can be measured and tuned after the line proves out. Committing to rotation structure now would complicate station coupling and trade off the throughput that is the primary large-stable-demand goal.

routes.route: Full chassis-scale moving-flow pilot before any further subassembly optimization
routes.reason: The only validated evidence is subassembly-scale. Scale-up to a whole chassis is the decisive test of uneven task times and largest-size conveyance limits. A single pilot line on actual production volume is the fastest discriminating experiment.
